subject: Quick Neighborhood Development Comments
comment: Hi Jonathon, I don't know that I have strong feelings on the proposed developments (and hence have taken a long time to chime in), but I thought I'd just go on the record to flesh out the pool of responses you're getting. It seems like the clustered proposal is untenable to anyone locally and the city, despite its desires for more development, is unlikely to push this one (and maybe it is simply more of a negotiating tactic; I don't remember what exactly the origins of this plan were). It seems to be inconsistent with the current state of infrastructure and locals are very hostile to it. Now, if the city did really want to push this, I would think it would be necessary for them to simultaneously articulate the changes they want to make to infrastructure to make this feasible (and not just in a, yeah, we have some ideas about how to address this -- actual maps, plans, proposals, cost estimates, etc.). When it comes to the mixed vs. original proposal, I don't have the strongest of feelings. It seems like at the heart of the debate are two issues: congestion and culture. For me, I don't have much to say on the culture front, to be honest. I know people have strong feelings about this, but I don't think either side has the moral right (unless you get into past promises/expectations, etc.); there are just two different dogmas. Many locally feel like there is a certain culture and way of life that should be preserved in Provo, yet the city views this as cover for NIMBYism (which is surely true in some part for some persons). The city feels dogmatically about providing sufficient housing and certain development principles including having mixed housing, yet locals perceive an emotional distance and disconnect (the council members really failed empathy 101 from what I could overhear from the Zoom call while juggling kids) and perhaps alternative interests that undermine the city's position. I actually think the city could make a potentially compelling case for their vision if they would spend the time and energy to both (a) back their dogmas with empirical evidence (which does exist in some forms) and (b) transparently lay out a vision for the whole city and how we fit into that and what infrastructure reforms will be made to support their vision. To be honest, some of the local arguments made for the West side culture felt counteproductive to their cause and cringe-worthy to an outsider (and even to some other locals). The hard thing in this case is that the stakes feel so small and the city seems to be trying to send a message more broadly with a small stakes issue; I perceive the overall threat to the West side culture or the overall gains from the mixed development to be significantly overstated by both parties. It seems like neither side wants to back down for fear of ceding ground in the next conflict (though it does seem like a bit of a dance, since, should the city plow ahead with more dense housing out West, the exact recourse available to locals on the West side is admittedly unclear to me). That said, even though the "macro" congestion from the mixed vs. the original development is unlikely to be large overall (at least so it would seem, though the city could have made it clearer what the estimates would be from this), the "micro" congestion to locals is potentially highly significant. Whether it's street parking, dangers to children from added traffic, etc. it seems like the details of the new developments can matter a lot for people living nearby. What's hard to separate is safety and efficiency from nuisance (which is not to be overlooked either), but the city has felt aloof on this point. In this sense, I'm inclined to defer to those living on 3000 W and Lakeshore barring the city providing a detailed estimate of how congestion would change (they did not seem prepared with such info, but maybe I missed that in the meeting). Since the big picture stakes are small, but the small stakes for those adjacent to the development are potentially large, it seems to argue in favor of the original development. But again, the city could try to make a more compelling case here if they would present more estimates. That said, maybe the city feels like there is no amount of effort possible to move people on this issue and so they don't feel that time spent is worth it (though it would help their credibility a lot dynamically). Anyway, all that to say, like the vast majority, I come down on the side of the original development plan, but I think it's not by a large margin and it could be changed if the city would do due diligence on the full impacts of the mixed development instead of the original one. I'm largely turned off by the culture battle though, and I think both sides would benefit from more understanding and perspective (the city having a coherent big picture vision would help here a lot). Thanks for all the hard work you put into this! Best, Christian

subject: Fort Utah Neighborhood Meeting
comment: May 5, 2021 Fort Utah Neighborhood Meeting Land Development/Planning Provo City Dear Neighborhood Representative, I would like to bring to your attention the Osprey nests/habitats which are located within the development around/near Lakeshore drive (just West of 3000 West). These birds have nested in this area for years. They were displaced when the earthmovers, drillers, pilings, etc., were employed to build Lakeshore Drive road/bridge but are now back (just this year). This new development will not only disrupt the Ospreys for now but will upset their environment for years to come, most likely never to return. We also have pheasants, geese, migratory birds close by that will be disrupted as well. Also, the earthmovers disturb the field mice. Each time the dirt is disturbed, we see more and more mice. Additionally, the trails and roads need to be clear of debri so Ryan can move around the area in his wheelchair. Thanks Much -- Terry ...as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Joshua 24:15
